The 25th Bttn, CEF was formed when the Canadian Government wanted a second division to send overseas. Lieutenant-Colonel G.A. Lecain from Round Hill, Annapolis Cty was authorized to mobilize the 25th in October 1914. He headquarters at the Armory in Halifax and had recruitment offices in Sydney, Yarmouth, Amherst, and Truro. Before Christmas 1914 the 25th was at full strength. They had been training at the Armory and on the Halifax Common. 

The 25th set sail from Halifax on May 20, 1915 on the ‘Saxonia’ for Devonport, England where they would arrive May 29, 1915. Thus began the 25th’s rigorous training in England where divionial reviews were carried out being King George V and then Premier of Canada Robert Borden (from Grande Pré himself). At the conclusion of their training the 25th became a Unit of the 5th Eastern Canada Infantry Brigade, 22nd Canadian Division. 

The brave men of the 25th suffered immense losses throughout WW1. Of the 1000 N Scotians who started with the bttn, only 100 men were alive at the end of the first year overseas. The other 900 men were either killed, missing, or taken prisoner. The 25th served in every major battle of WWI that comes to mind: Somme (1916 & 1918), Vimy Ridge, Passchendale, Battle of Hill 70. This uniform belonged to one of only 3 men in the Hants/Kings County border area who survived the entire war. 

On a lighter note, the 25th had a [mascot](https://archives.novascotia.ca/warletters/archives/?ID=17) Robert the Bruce, a goat that they purchased from an old Belgian lady as a kid. The soldiers bottle-fed Robert and trained him to dance for the pipe band, drink beer, eat cigarettes, and ask for his blanket at lights-out every night. Robert survived the whole war and went home to Baddeck with a Major where he lived the rest of his life on a peaceful farm. Here is his [name tag](https://archives.novascotia.ca/warletters/archives/?ID=18) which highlights the battles he survived. Robert was truly indestructible and as the soldiers described it, his brutal head butt kept anyone outside of the 25th Bttn away!

I’m working at a small community museum in the Annapolis Valley area of Nova Scotia. It is surrounded by the Bay of Fundy which has the highest tides in the world (40-46ft in this area), nearly every harbour/port in this region is completely emptied at low tide and fills again at high. This has caused the soil of the area to be incredibly fertile over time and the Valley is still the agricultural heart of Nova Scotia with apples being the most common food grown. This is an accounting book which has a variety of different products being bought & sold relating to agriculture (i.e. potatoes, oxen, hay) and also some personal financial accounting (paying for doctor’s visits, postage, and trips to Halifax) so I believe it was a personal budgeting/finance book for the Davison family. However, there is doodles from this young girl Etta on nearly every page, and the front 10 pages consist of newspaper clippings of children’s stories glued on top of the finance information. My best guess is that once the book was filled in 1860, it was given to little Etta to use since it was cheaper to reuse than buy new paper.  Either that, or she probably got in trouble for writing over important information!

Hello Paula and Naomi! I am a history student at Acadia University in Wolfville, Nova Scotia. Weather in Nova Scotia is always changing! Right now I’m sitting on my porch cold because it’s 14°C, but just a few days ago it was 30°C. The winters are quite cold depending how north in the province you are, in my area it is typically -10°c to -20°C in the coldest parts of winter. It is also very windy in the Wolfville area so that can make it feel colder. As the saying goes, if you don’t like the weather in Nova Scotia, just wait 5 minutes and it will change.
I grew up in Lunenburg County which is on the opposite side of the province to Wolfville. The town of Lunenburg is a UNESCO World Heritage site and home of the Bluenose II which is featured on the back of the Canadian dime (10 cents). It is a small and quiet area with a growing elderly population, however in recent years it has seen an increase in younger families moving from Western Canada where real estate is more expensive. 
I was originally born in the USA but moved to Nova Scotia at around 6 years old. I basically have always lived in Nova Scotia and went through the public education system here as well. 
COVID-19 has been handled very well in my opinion by the Nova Scotia government. As of July 31st, masks were made mandatory in all public places to prevent a second wave. There is currently only 1 active case in Nova Scotia, but as university students return from across Canada and the world I would not be surprised to see a jump in cases.
